title: Chayei Sarah: meditating in the field (Genesis 24:63)
hook: Isaac goes out "to meditate in the field"; the Talmud says he began the afternoon prayer (Berakhot 26b)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a servant at a well, and Rebekah coming out before he'd finished. Your line was ask plainly.

Late afternoon is a strange hour. The work isn't done, the evening hasn't started, and the light goes gold and long across the parking lot. Most of us push straight through it, answering one more email. Meanwhile, the servant is bringing Rebekah home on a camel. And Isaac, the son she's coming to marry, isn't waiting by the tent. He's out in a field, alone, as the day turns. Today: the prayer that lives in that in-between hour.
screen: `THE GOLDEN, IN-BETWEEN HOUR.` → `REBEKAH ON HER WAY.` → `ISAAC, ALONE IN A FIELD.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." The Hebrew word for meditate is lasuach, and nobody is completely sure what it means: to walk, to think, to talk to yourself. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, reads it as prayer, and connects the three daily prayers to the three fathers. Abraham began the morning prayer, when he rose early and stood before God. Isaac began the afternoon prayer, here in the field. Jacob began the evening prayer, on the night he stopped to sleep on the road. The same page gives another view: the prayers stand in for the daily offerings in the Temple. Both views are still taught. The afternoon prayer is called Mincha, which means a gift, or an offering; it was the name of the afternoon offering of grain. Mincha is short, often ten minutes or so, and it falls right in the middle of the working day. That's part of the point. Morning prayer comes at the start of things; evening prayer comes when they're over. Mincha asks you to stop while everything is still going. The Talmud says to be careful with it, because the prophet Elijah was answered at the time of the afternoon offering. Then look at the story. Isaac lifts his eyes, and there are camels coming. Rebekah lifts her eyes, sees him, and gets down from her camel. The two meet for the first time just after he has stepped out to pray, in the field, at evening.
screen: `ISAAC WENT OUT TO MEDITATE.` · `THREE FATHERS, THREE PRAYERS.` · `MINCHA: A GIFT, MID-DAY.` · `HE LIFTS HIS EYES: CAMELS.` · then, large: `THE FIELD AT EVENING.`

segments.voice: Step outside or to a window if you can; if it isn't afternoon where you are, picture that long gold light. Stand still, feel the air, and notice what the light is doing on the ground; you don't need words. If you pray, this is the hour Isaac chose, and you can speak to God in whatever words come.
Mincha. A gift, or an offering: the afternoon prayer, which the Talmud traces back to Isaac, meditating in the field.
Your line: the field at evening. A pause in the middle of things. That's day one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Many observant Jews say Mincha each afternoon, anytime from just after midday until sunset, often with a quick minyan at work, at school or in a synagogue on the way home.
